name: Adam Ibrahim

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. What you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run three CNC mills at Wescott Precision, cutting aluminium brackets for aircraft seats. Mornings I load the programs, check the first part with the micrometer and the coordinate machine, and then it's tool changes and watching for chatter. I'm a team lead, so I also sign off the shift sheet and sort out who covers who. By two o'clock my back tells me it's been a long day.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: And how do new tools usually reach you on the floor?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Slowly, and I'm fine with that. I'll try something once the lads on the next shift have tried it and it hasn't broken a tool. Lately I ask a chatbot to explain a bit of G-code I don't recognise, which has saved me a phone call or two.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's useful in small ways, like a calculator was. At work I'd tell the younger ones to try it for paperwork but never trust it on a tolerance. Online I wouldn't say much at all.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, the chatbot saves me twenty minutes a day at most, and it doesn't touch knowing why a cut is chattering. That's the part that matters. I think the next few years look like the last few.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing what I do, maybe use the chatbot a bit more to write the shift handover notes. We have a refit of one mill due next spring and I'd carry on as planned. And I'd keep paying down the last of the car loan, nothing dramatic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. If this is all there is, I'm well placed to see out my last four years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you use a chatbot sometimes. What for exactly?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly to read a strange error code, or to rewrite an email to a supplier so I don't sound cross. I wouldn't let it near a program until someone I trust has proved it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does your union come into it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, I pay my dues and I vote on the safety stuff. I'd bring up with the union reps that the extra software shouldn't become extra targets for us.

say: It's a useful **small** tool, like a calculator was.
I tell younger staff to try it for paperwork but never for tolerances.
think: The chatbot saves me **twenty minutes** a day at most.
The next few years look much like the last few.
do: Use the chatbot to write shift **handover** notes.
Carry on with the planned mill refit next spring.
Pay off the last of the **car loan**.
feel: **Calm**, and well placed to see out my last four years.
S0.quote: The chatbot saves me twenty minutes a day at most, and it doesn't touch knowing why a cut is chattering.
fieldNote: Pragmatic user of AI, with firm limits at **tolerances**.
Secure on money and time, so calm is earned.
Cautious not resistant: tries things once others have.

steps.text: Use the chatbot to draft shift handover notes
Keep running the three mills through the spring refit
Pay off the car loan by the new year

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the planning side is next to go. We have two programmers and a scheduler, and I'm sure a smart program could do half their day. The floor would change slower; a mill still needs somebody to set the fixture and listen to it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully it makes me a bit uneasy, not for me but for our programmers. Haroun does the CAM programming for a whole cell and he's 31 with a baby. If the firm needs one programmer instead of three, he's the one I'd worry for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get properly stuck into the AI tools, since that's where the firm will look. I'd ask to be sent on the supplier's course for the new programming software, and I'd learn how to check its output on the machine. Money-wise I'd keep a bit more in the account than usual.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. I'm fine, but the mood in the break room would turn.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about at Wescott?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The programmers and the scheduler, then the inspection staff once cameras get good enough. I'd suggest we put them on the floor beside me so they pick up both skills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you move faster on the AI tools in that world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, definitely. If the proven tool is there, I'll learn it. The ones who ignore it end up being the ones the firm quietly stops asking.

say: The **planning** side goes first, and the floor changes slower.
A mill still needs somebody to set the fixture and listen to it.
think: I worry for **Haroun** (our 31-year-old programmer) with a baby at home.
I'm fine myself, but the break-room mood will turn.
do: Ask to go on the supplier's **course** for the new programming software.
Learn to check the AI's output on the machine.
Keep a bit more in the **account** than usual.
feel: **Uneasy**; I'm fine, but those around me are not.
S1.quote: A mill still needs somebody to set the fixture and listen to it.
fieldNote: He sees the **thinking** work as the exposed part and his own as slower to change.
Concern is for named, younger colleagues.
Moves on tools once proven, as his profile says.

steps.text: Ask to go on the supplier's course for the new programming software
Learn to check machine programs written by AI against the real part
Keep three months more wages than usual in the account

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we'd need government help fast, because it's two years and nobody's ready. Wescott would be tempted to cut programmers and planners at once and move on the hands-on work as soon as a robot could load a mill. I'd tell my union rep to ask for a transition deal now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, 2028 is the office jobs and 2031 is mine. I'd be 63 then, and I could probably hang on if the firm keeps a few of us who know the fixtures. But it would be close, and I wouldn't bet on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get stuck into AI tools at once, take any course the firm pays for, and aim to be the person who supervises the robot cells. I'd cut spending a bit, keep my savings and make a plan for retiring at 62 if the offer's decent. I'd talk to Salma, my wife, about where we'd live.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I know I've got a cushion, but it would be the end of a trade I've done for forty years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the plant owners do first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pay for a robot to do the easy brackets first, the long runs. The odd, tricky parts stay with us longer. I'd try to be the one who sets up the odd, tricky parts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who else is on your mind?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My daughter's thinking about her own job in logistics. I'd tell her to get close to the technology, not away from it.

say: We need **government help** fast, because nobody's ready in two years.
I'd ask my union rep for a transition deal now.
think: 2028 hits the office jobs and **2031** hits mine.
I could hang on at 63, but I wouldn't bet on it.
do: Take any **AI course** the firm pays for and aim to supervise the robot cells.
Plan to retire at **62** if the offer is decent.
Cut spending a little and talk to Salma about where we'd live.
feel: **Anxious**; it would end a trade I've done for forty years.
S2.quote: 2028 is the office jobs and 2031 is mine. I'd be 63 then, and I could probably hang on
fieldNote: He separates the **thinking** and robot timelines clearly, without being prompted to.
Plans a pivot to supervising robots rather than resisting.
Retirement offer at 62 is his fallback.

steps.text: Take every AI and robot-cell course the firm will pay for
Ask HR for the retirement offer at 62
Cut eating out and holidays to build a bigger cushion
Ask the union rep for a transition deal in writing

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years feels more manageable. I'd say we should start now, with training for the younger lads first. At work I'd push for a shared plan so nobody gets surprised in 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Quietly, I think I'd be able to get through to retirement in this one. Robots come in 2034, I'd be 66 by then, and I'm planning to stop at 62 or 63 anyway. The ones I'd worry about are in their thirties.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start learning the AI tools now rather than later. I'd offer to teach the apprentices how to prove a program on the machine, because that's the skill that still matters. And I'd fix the flat's roof while I still have wages.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but steadier than the first one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell the younger ones at work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Learn to work with the machines, but also have something to fall back on. Salma's niece did nursing and I'd say she's the safer one of the two.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your daughter?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my daughter to get close to the technology, not away from it, and to keep some savings that don't depend on one employer.

say: Five years is **manageable** if we start training the younger lads now.
I'd push for a shared plan so nobody is surprised in 2034.
think: Quietly, I think I'd get through to **retirement** in this one without trouble.
The ones I worry about are the colleagues in their thirties.
do: Learn the AI tools now rather than later.
Teach the **apprentices** how to prove a program on the machine.
Fix the flat's **roof** while I still have wages.
feel: **Uneasy**, but steadier than in the two-year picture.
S3.quote: I'd tell my daughter to get close to the technology, not away from it, and to keep some savings that don't depend on one employer.
fieldNote: Time lets him move from worry to **teaching** the apprentices.
Retirement age protects him, and he knows it.
Advice for his daughter shows his values: adapt, but hold a cushion.

steps.text: Practice with the AI programming tools every week from now
Teach the apprentices how to prove a program on the machine
Pay for the flat's roof repairs from this year's wages
Talk my daughter through safe jobs and building savings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years is generous. I'd say it gives everyone the chance to do it right, with retraining paid for by the firms that gain. I'd be glad about it, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'll have been retired for eight years by then. It's the lads I think about. If the 2036 date holds, a 30-year-old today has time to become the person who oversees these systems.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working to 62, maybe 63, then do part-time teaching at the college for the machining course. I'd spend time on the allotment too. And I'd keep helping Haroun learn the tools, because he'll need them longer than I will.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. It's the kind of timeline that lets me finish my working life as I planned.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell the young people at Wescott?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them the job won't look like mine, but there's a place for people who understand how a part is really cut. They should stay curious and not wait for the firm to hand it over.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you think ten years is enough time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the date holds, ten years is enough time for a proper deal between unions, government and firms.

say: Ten years lets everyone do it right, with **retraining** paid for by the firms that gain.
I'd be glad about it, honestly, and I'd say so at work.
think: I'll be retired for eight years by 2036, so it's the **lads** I think about.
A 30-year-old today has time to learn to oversee these systems.
do: Work to **62** or 63 and then teach part-time at the college.
Keep helping Haroun learn the new tools.
Spend more time on the allotment.
feel: **Calm**; I get to finish my working life as planned.
S4.quote: If the 2036 date holds, a 30-year-old today has time to become the person who oversees these systems.
fieldNote: Long horizon gives him a **teaching** role he warms to.
His calm comes from retirement timing, not from belief the change is small.

steps.text: Work until 62 or 63, then retire on the full pension
Teach part-time on the college machining course
Coach Haroun on the new tools every month
Help my daughter plan her studies for the next ten years

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. Not because I'd lose my job first, but because there'd be no time to get ready and the young ones would pay for it. What would help is a government deal that pays for retraining and a firm that tells us the plan early.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that I'm not afraid of the machines. I've had a pocket calculator and a chatbot and a coordinate machine. It's the speed that scares me, and who gets looked after when it comes.

headlineQuote: I'm not afraid of the machines. I've had a pocket calculator and a chatbot and a coordinate machine.
portrait: Adam (**58**, team lead on CNC mills making aircraft seat brackets) is a steady, cautious adopter with strong savings.
He uses a chatbot **now and then** for G-code and emails, and sets clear limits where tolerances are concerned.
His worries are for younger colleagues like Haroun and for his daughter, not for his own retirement.
He grows more anxious as AGI comes closer, but a clear **plan** and time keep him steady.
biggestWorry: The **2028** scenario worries him because there'd be no time for the young ones to prepare.
whatWouldHelp: A government **deal** paying for retraining, and an employer who shares the plan early.
